researchNotes.title: What Velociraptor really looked like
researchNotes.text: Velociraptor was much smaller than movies show. It was only about 1.5 to 2 meters long (roughly 5 to 7 feet) and weighed about 15 to 20 kilograms (33 to 43 pounds) -- roughly the size of a large turkey. It stood about half a meter tall at the hip. In the Jurassic Park films, the animals shown were modeled on the larger relative Deinonychus and were about twice the real size. Velociraptor walked on two legs and had a long, stiff tail that helped it balance and steer when running fast.

researchNotes.title: Velociraptor had feathers
researchNotes.text: Velociraptor was covered in feathers, much like modern birds. In 2007, scientists found quill knobs on the forearm bone of a Velociraptor fossil from Mongolia -- these are the bumps where feathers attach on bird wing bones. Close relatives like Microraptor and Zhenyuanlong have been found with preserved feather impressions, providing strong evidence that the whole family was feathered. Despite having feathered arms, Velociraptor could not fly. Its wings were too small and its feathers were symmetrical (flying birds have asymmetrical feathers). The feathers likely helped keep it warm (since it was warm-blooded) and may have been used for display to attract mates, or to cover eggs while nesting.

researchNotes.title: The famous sickle claw
researchNotes.text: Velociraptor's most famous feature was the large, curved, sickle-shaped claw on the second toe of each foot. This claw could grow to over 6.5 centimeters (about 2.5 inches) around its outer edge. Velociraptor walked on only two of its three toes, keeping the sickle claw raised off the ground to keep it sharp. Scientists once thought this claw was used to slash open prey, but research (including building a mechanical model) showed it was more likely used as a stabbing and gripping tool -- much like an eagle's talon -- to pin down prey and prevent it from escaping.

researchNotes.title: What Velociraptor ate
researchNotes.text: Velociraptor was a carnivore (meat-eater) with lots of sharp, pointed, backward-curving teeth. Its narrow jaws and lightweight build suggest it mostly hunted small animals like mammals and lizards that would have been easy to catch and overpower. It may have occasionally hunted small, young dinosaurs. One fossil was found with a pterosaur bone inside the Velociraptor's body, suggesting it sometimes scavenged (ate animals that were already dead). Like most predators, Velociraptor probably ate whatever it could find.

researchNotes.title: A fast runner
researchNotes.text: Velociraptor's name means 'swift thief' or 'quick plunderer' in Latin. It lived up to this name -- scientists estimate it could run at over 40 kilometers per hour (25 miles per hour) in short bursts, which is faster than the fastest human sprinter. It had long, muscular legs with relatively long shins, which gave it a longer stride. Its stiff tail acted like a rudder, helping it make quick turns at high speed. However, it was not the fastest dinosaur -- that title goes to the ornithomimosaurs, which resembled ostriches.

researchNotes.title: How smart was Velociraptor
researchNotes.text: Velociraptor had a relatively large brain compared to its body size, making it one of the smarter dinosaurs. However, it was not as clever as shown in the Jurassic Park movies. Scientists compare its intelligence to that of an average bird, perhaps like a hawk. It was smart enough to be an effective hunter, but not smart enough to outsmart humans or solve complex problems like crows or parrots can.

researchNotes.title: Where Velociraptor lived
researchNotes.text: Velociraptor lived in what is now Mongolia and northern China during the Late Cretaceous period, about 75 to 71 million years ago. Its environment was dry and sandy, with sand dunes and occasional streams -- similar to a desert. The fossils were found in the Djadochta Formation and Bayan Mandahu Formation. The landscape would have been harsh and hot, quite different from the lush jungles shown in movies.

researchNotes.title: Discovery of the first Velociraptor
researchNotes.text: The first Velociraptor fossil was discovered on August 11, 1923, during an American Museum of Natural History expedition to the Flaming Cliffs (Bayanzag) in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia. Peter Kaisen found a crushed but complete skull with a claw. In 1924, Henry Fairfield Osborn named the new dinosaur Velociraptor mongoliensis. The name comes from the Latin words 'velox' (swift) and 'raptor' (robber or plunderer). Since then, over a dozen fossil skeletons have been found.

researchNotes.title: The Fighting Dinosaurs fossil
researchNotes.text: One of the most famous fossils ever found shows a Velociraptor locked in combat with a Protoceratops, a small plant-eating dinosaur. Discovered in 1971 in Mongolia, this remarkable fossil captures the two animals frozen in battle: the Velociraptor's sickle claw is in the Protoceratops's throat, while the Velociraptor's arm is crushed in the Protoceratops's beak. They were likely buried alive by a collapsing sand dune or sandstorm during their fight. This fossil is considered a national treasure of Mongolia.

researchNotes.title: Velociraptor vs. movies
researchNotes.text: Velociraptor is one of the most famous dinosaurs thanks to the Jurassic Park movies, but the films got many things wrong. The movie raptors were about twice the real size, had no feathers, and could open doors -- none of which is true. The movie creatures were actually modeled on Deinonychus, a larger relative. Shortly after the first film was released in 1993, an even bigger raptor called Utahraptor was discovered, which was closer to the movie size. The real Velociraptor was more like a strange, toothy, feathered bird of prey that happened to live on the ground.

researchNotes.title: Velociraptor's relatives and the link to birds
researchNotes.text: Velociraptor belongs to a family of dinosaurs called dromaeosaurids, which are among the closest dinosaur relatives of modern birds. All dromaeosaurids had feathers, sickle claws, and relatively large brains. The family ranged from tiny Microraptor (about the size of a crow) to enormous Utahraptor (about the size of a polar bear). Velociraptor sat in the middle of this range. Modern birds are living dinosaurs, and studying Velociraptor helps scientists understand how dinosaurs evolved into the birds we see today.

handoffNotes: For a 5-year-old audience, the most engaging angles are: (1) Velociraptor was turkey-sized, not movie-monster-sized; (2) it had feathers like a bird; (3) it had a special claw on its foot; (4) it was fast. The fighting dinosaurs fossil is represented by a size comparison diagram rather than the actual fossil photo, which was too confusing for this age. The cassowary photo provides a strong modern-bird-to-dinosaur visual connection. The sickle claw comparison and foot model images give close-up detail views. The image pool mixes illustrations and photos but keeps a coherent, colorful, child-friendly feel. Avoid scary hunting scenes for this age band.
